title: Summit Retail — Inference budget & deployment options discovery
summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics, batching and caching levers, and decision criteria for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer emphasized cost sensitivity for high QPS storefront use, strict data residency / encryption needs for PII, and desire for an initial POC to run sample latencies and unit-costs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — we're Maya from Redwood, Carlos our SE, and Liam in solutions. Quick intros?
[00:12] Priya Raman: Hey all, I'm Priya, head of AI at Summit Retail. We run recommendation and chat assistant on the web and mobile.
[00:20] Jonas Le: Jonas, platform eng, I manage infra and cost dashboards.
[00:25] Aisha Khan: Aisha, CISO — I'll be looking at compliance and data flow.
[00:31] Carlos Ortega: Great — today we want to understand your traffic profile, success criteria and give you a sense for unit economics across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Quick agenda: current stack & traffic, cost levers (batching/caching/quant), deployment constraints (VPC, on-prem), then a recommended POC.
[00:52] Priya Raman: Sounds good. At a high level we do ~250 req/s at peak for recommendations, average prompt 120 tokens input, 300 tokens output. We have bursty traffic during promotions — 3x for a few hours.
[01:10] Jonas Le: We're very cost sensitive; if unit token cost is too high the product math breaks. We also want <200ms response for search-as-you-type and <600ms for personalized recommendations.
[01:24] Carlos Ortega: Ok. For that traffic profile, the obvious levers are batching, prefix/KV caching for repeated sessions, and routing to model variants. Hosted gives fastest time-to-value but you pay per-token; Dedicated reduces per-token infra cost but requires commit. Private adds control for residency and KMS.
[01:41] Marco Diaz: Can you give ballpark per-token numbers? Even ranges?
[01:46] Maya Chen: Sure — rough public-ish examples (these are illustrative): for a high-quality hosted model at low-latency, think $0.0008 - $0.0012 per generated token in pure hosted unit terms; lower-tier open variants can be $0.0002 - $0.0005 per token. Dedicated can drop your effective infra-backed per-token to a fraction — maybe 3x-5x improvement depending on utilization and batch efficiency.
[02:10] Jonas Le: 3x-5x is big. What's the utilization threshold to get that?
[02:15] Carlos Ortega: You need steady utilization — typically >40–50% to amortize reserved GPUs. Peak-burst patterns make autoscale/burst important. Redwood Dedicated supports autoscaling and burst pools to handle promos while keeping base commit lower.
[02:29] Aisha Khan: On compliance — we need encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS, audit logs and SOC2. Any issues with hosted?
[02:37] Maya Chen: Hosted supports SOC2 and we can integrate customer KMS on Dedicated/Private. Hosted keeps logs but for strict residency and full control you usually pick Private with our private control plane or on-prem package.
[02:52] Priya Raman: We may need on-prem for a subset of PII workloads; other anonymized inference can be hosted.
[02:58] Carlos Ortega: That's a common hybrid pattern — route sensitive workloads to Private or Dedicated with VPC and keep lower-risk workloads on Hosted.
[03:06] Jonas Le: Tell me more about caching — prefix cache vs KV? We have many repeated prefixes in recommendation prompts.
[03:12] Carlos Ortega: Prefix/prompt caching keeps full token sequence outputs for identical inputs; KV cache keeps model KV cache to speed autoregression when sessions repeat. For recommendations where user context repeats across requests, prefix caching can give huge token reductions, especially for output-heavy prompts.
[03:27] Maya Chen: Practically you'll see 20–60% token savings if you can cache common prefixes, depends on variability. We run a quick fingerprinting test in POC to estimate that.
[03:38] Priya Raman: And batching? Our interactive use wants low latency, but recommendations could tolerate a bit more.
[03:44] Carlos Ortega: Continuous batching can be tuned — you set latency SLOs and the runtime optimizes batch formation. For search-as-you-type you likely want minimal batching; for recommendations you can batch aggressively and save cost. Redwood's routing can send requests to different pools by route, model, or latency tier.
[03:58] Jonas Le: Are there examples of customers splitting by route?
[04:02] Maya Chen: Yes — retail customers send personalization to Dedicated with higher batch windows and keep cart-checkout to Hosted low-latency lane.
[04:10] Aisha Khan: What about fallback if Dedicated is saturated? We need graceful degradation.
[04:15] Carlos Ortega: We have automatic fallback policies: route to a compatible hosted variant or another region. You can specify acceptable model variants and max added latency.
[04:24] Marco Diaz: How accurate are the quality differences between variants? We can't lose conversion by using cheaper models.
[04:29] Maya Chen: Part of POC is A/B on a holdout set. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and model variants and run evals against your prompts to show quality deltas.
[04:40] Jonas Le: Can you walk through an example POC scope?
[04:44] Carlos Ortega: Example POC: 2 weeks, run a 10% traffic mirror for recommendation route, measure latency, tokens/sec, cache-hit, and cost. We'll instrument token-level breakdown and provide a model/cost report. We'll also run sample stress bursts to validate autoscale.
[05:00] Priya Raman: How much effort to mirror? We run on GCP — do you support GCP endpoints?
[05:06] Maya Chen: Yes, hosted is cloud-agnostic for customers. For Dedicated/Private we'd provision in your chosen region/cloud; Private can be VPC-connected. Our SE team can provide a small traffic-mirroring snippet and SDKs.
[05:16] Jonas Le: About cost reporting — we need token-level and route-level dashboards and alerts when spend exceeds X.
[05:21] Maya Chen: Redwood Console gives token-level costs, route/model breakdowns, and alerting hooks. We can connect to your billing pipeline as well.
[05:28] Aisha Khan: Network diagrams and data flow — please send; we need to review for our network/compliance team.
[05:33] Maya Chen: We'll attach our architecture diagram and a private-deployment network spec.
[05:38] Priya Raman: Any gotchas with quantization and accuracy? We worry cheaping out will reduce conversion.
[05:44] Carlos Ortega: Quantization is model-dependent. Redwood's Optimize recommends quantization profiles per-workload; we run evals to ensure quality is within an agreed tolerance. Sometimes int8 works fine for ranking, not for creative copy.
[05:57] Marco Diaz: Pricing model for Dedicated — is it flat monthly + usage?
[06:01] Maya Chen: Dedicated has committed capacity pricing — a base monthly for reserved GPUs + usage adjustments for burst. We'll give an example quote matched to your expected QPS and utilization.
[06:10] Jonas Le: If we do Private on VPC, what are the lead times?
[06:13] Maya Chen: Private lead time varies — small VPC-based private cluster can be a few weeks for onboarding, larger on-prem can be months. We tailor by scope.
[06:22] Jonas Le: Who are typical decision stakeholders and procurement timeline?
[06:25] Priya Raman: For us: AI/Product decide on quality, Platform signs off on cost/ops, Security signs for compliance. Procurement sometimes needs a quarter lead time for contracts. We aim to decide within 6–8 weeks.
[06:38] Maya Chen: That's helpful. Any specific SLA needs?
[06:41] Aisha Khan: We want 99.9% for Dedicated critical routes, and detailed audit logs retained 1 year. Also SSO (SAML) and RBAC.
[06:50] Carlos Ortega: Dedicated SLA can be discussed; RBAC and SAML supported, and audit retention is configurable via add-on.
[06:57] Priya Raman: Can we run a quick cost example? If we assume 250 req/s, avg 420 tokens total, 3x promotions, what's rough monthly token count and cost?
[07:05] Carlos Ortega: Quick back-of-envelope — baseline 250 rpm? Let me calculate — 250 req/s * 3600s * 24 * 30 is huge, but many of those are during business hours; for a rough monthly active: say 250 req/s 10 hours/day * 20 days * 3600 = ~180M requests; multiply by 420 tokens = 75.6B tokens. At $0.0006/token hosted that'd be $45.3M — obviously huge.
[07:32] (general chuckle)
[07:34] Maya Chen: Exactly why batching/cache/dedicated matter — with 50% cache-hit and batching and dedicated you'd bring that dramatically down. Also many requests are smaller — this is a worst-case calc.
[07:44] Jonas Le: Ok that highlights the problem. We can't operate with hosted-only at those numbers.
[07:48] Priya Raman: So what's realistic POC size? We can't mirror full production.
[07:52] Carlos Ortega: Common approach: 5–10% mirror of peak for 2 weeks to capture cache-hit and latency. We'll simulate the promo burst in stress tests.
[07:59] Marco Diaz: Are there any contracts for data retention or delete requests?
[08:04] Maya Chen: Yes — we support data retention policies and can delete customer data on demand; Private gives the most straightforward control.
[08:10] Aisha Khan: What about encryption keys — do you manage KMS or customer-managed?
[08:14] Carlos Ortega: Customer-managed KMS is supported on Dedicated and Private; for Hosted we have managed keys but offer strong guarantees and options.
[08:22] Jonas Le: Competitors — are there any features Redwood provides that make Dedicated easier?
[08:27] Maya Chen: Our autoscale with burst pools and the unified API across Hosted/Dedicated/Private is a big differentiator. Also built-in token-level observability and Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization.
[08:39] Priya Raman: Can you email a sample cost model with variable knobs — batch windows, cache hit %, model variant?
[08:45] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll send a spreadsheet with knobs and a worked example.
[08:49] Marco Diaz: On the contract side, trial period or credits?
[08:52] Maya Chen: We usually offer trial credits and a POC pricing proposal. For Dedicated pilots we often do a short-term reserved with credits applied.
[08:59] (brief pause)
[09:02] Carlos Ortega: Quick tech note — if you have session affinity in recommendations, KV cache savings can be 30–70% for autoregressive cost. We'll instrument that in POC.
[09:12] Aisha Khan: We'll need an MOU or NDA before sharing some telemetry.
[09:15] Maya Chen: We can provide that; our standard NDA is fine.
[09:19] Jonas Le: Ok great. Timeline wise we can kick a POC in about 3 weeks pending contract.
[09:24] Priya Raman: Decision criteria: 1) <x cost per active user, 2) latency SLOs for specific routes, 3) security controls met.
[09:33] Maya Chen: Noted. Anything else on the deep technical side?
[09:36] Carlos Ortega: We might want to run a short model-eval on your test prompts to show quality delta between candidate variants. That helps set thresholds.
[09:44] Marco Diaz: Yes please.
[09:46] Maya Chen: Ok quick recap and next steps — we'll: 1) send pricing spreadsheet with knobs, 2) send SOC2, network diagrams, NDA, 3) propose POC scope and timeline, 4) schedule technical onboarding with SEs for mirroring.
[09:59] Priya Raman: Perfect. Who owns the POC proposal?
[10:02] Maya Chen: I'll own the commercial proposal, Carlos will own the technical POC plan.
[10:07] Jonas Le: Action on us — we'll prepare a small dataset and test prompts, and get procurement info.
[10:13] Aisha Khan: I'll coordinate the security review once you send docs.
[10:17] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials by EOD tomorrow and aim to have the kickoff calendar for week of Nov 16.
[10:25] Priya Raman: Thank you.
[47:30] (call ends)

Notes: transcript has typical transcription noise: some numbers approximated; proper nouns spelling may vary.
